sections.title: One medium, several speakers
sections.narration: Put three computers on one shared communication medium. Each has a message ready, and none owns the whole resource permanently. Who gets to transmit now? This is a medium-access problem, separate from choosing an Internet route. We will follow the rules that turn uncoordinated attempts into more useful communication under contention.
sections.takeaway: Medium access control decides how stations share a communication resource.

sections.title: Make overlap visible
sections.narration: Computer A begins sending, then computer B starts before A finishes. Their signals overlap at a receiver, making correct recovery of the frames impossible in our simple model. The glowing red region marks the conflict. Two drawn arrows crossing is only a visual symbol; actual collision behavior depends on the shared medium and receiver.
bullets: A receiver may lose both frames
sections.takeaway: A collision concerns overlapping signals at a receiver.

sections.title: Pure ALOHA: send when ready
sections.narration: The simplest rule is to transmit whenever data is ready. This is pure ALOHA. If success is not confirmed, the station waits a random interval and tries again. There is no global turn-taking schedule in this model. At low demand, attempts can succeed easily; more simultaneous demand creates more overlaps and repeated attempts.
sections.takeaway: Pure ALOHA allows a station to begin transmitting whenever data is ready.

sections.title: A vulnerable interval of 2T
sections.narration: Give every frame the same duration, T. Another frame beginning less than T before ours can still overlap its start; another beginning less than T after ours can overlap its end. Together, these possible interfering start times span two T. This vulnerable interval explains why even slightly offset attempts can cause trouble.
bullets: Conflicts can start before or after
sections.takeaway: For equal-length pure ALOHA frames, the vulnerable interval spans 2T.

sections.title: Why retry randomly?
sections.narration: After a collision, suppose both stations wait exactly one second. They may restart together and collide again. Choosing independent random retry delays makes repeated synchronization less likely. It does not guarantee that the next attempt succeeds. Follow two different waiting markers: one station gets a clear opportunity while the other continues waiting.
bullets: Identical waits can repeat a clash
sections.takeaway: Independent retry timing reduces the chance of repeated collisions.

sections.title: Slotted ALOHA adds boundaries
sections.narration: Now divide time into slots, each long enough for one of our equal-length frames. Stations may begin only at a slot boundary. They still compete: two choosing the same slot collide. But a station cannot begin halfway through an occupied slot. This extra timing agreement changes which transmission starts can overlap a frame.
sections.takeaway: Slotted ALOHA restricts transmission starts to common slot boundaries.

sections.title: The vulnerable interval becomes T
sections.narration: With perfectly aligned slots and our ideal assumptions, another attempt must choose the same slot to overlap this frame. The vulnerable start interval is therefore one T rather than two T. Real systems need timing coordination and account for propagation. Our clean slot diagram isolates the benefit of restricting when stations may begin.
sections.takeaway: Under the ideal slot model, the vulnerable interval is one slot.

sections.title: Interpret the ideal efficiency result
sections.narration: Under the classic equal-frame, Poisson-attempt model, pure ALOHA throughput is G times e to minus two G, while slotted throughput is G times e to minus G. Their maxima are approximately eighteen and thirty-seven percent. These are model results, not universal measurements for every wireless network or every offered traffic pattern.
sections.takeaway: The familiar ALOHA maxima depend on a specific ideal traffic model.

sections.title: Scheduling or contention?
sections.narration: Compare a reserved time schedule with ALOHA. Scheduled turns avoid collisions among compliant synchronized stations, but an idle station's reservation can waste an opportunity. Contention allows stations to compete when they have data, but collisions and retries consume resources. Different traffic loads and coordination constraints favor different tradeoffs; neither picture represents free bandwidth.
sections.takeaway: Collision reduction comes with assumptions or coordination costs.

sections.title: Listen before transmitting
sections.narration: Carrier Sense Multiple Access improves our rule by listening first. If a station senses the medium busy, it defers according to its protocol. If it appears idle, it may attempt transmission. This avoids some obvious overlaps, but the observation is local and signals take time to propagate. Listening alone cannot guarantee collision-free access.
bullets: Defer when the channel is busy
sections.takeaway: Carrier sensing can avoid transmissions that obviously conflict locally.

sections.title: A distant sender can still start
sections.narration: Place A and B far apart on the shared wire. A starts, but its signal has not reached B yet. B senses idle and starts too. Both followed the sensing rule, yet their signals collide. Animate the expanding signal fronts separately: a decision based on local silence is not instant knowledge of the entire cable.
bullets: Both ends may initially sense idle
sections.takeaway: Propagation delay allows collisions even with carrier sensing.

sections.title: One-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: In one-persistent CSMA, a ready station keeps sensing while the medium is busy and transmits when it becomes idle. If several stations are waiting, they can all seize that moment and collide. The name describes eagerness after sensing an idle medium; it does not mean continuing to transmit through an already detected conflict.
bullets: Transmit when the medium becomes idle
sections.takeaway: One-persistent stations transmit as soon as their sensed channel becomes idle.

sections.title: Nonpersistent CSMA
sections.narration: A nonpersistent station that finds the medium busy waits a random interval before sensing again. This reduces the chance that every waiting station transmits at the exact instant the channel clears. The tradeoff is extra delay: the channel might become free while a station is still waiting before its next sensing attempt.
sections.takeaway: Nonpersistent waiting reduces synchronized attempts but can add idle delay.

sections.title: P-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: In a slotted p-persistent model, a station seeing an idle channel transmits with probability p, or defers to another slot with probability one minus p. The choice spreads attempts, but selecting p requires assumptions about contention. Do not confuse these probability-based starts with the randomly chosen backoff interval after an Ethernet collision.
sections.takeaway: P-persistent CSMA makes a probabilistic choice at an idle slot.

sections.title: Add detection on historical Ethernet
sections.narration: Historical shared, half-duplex Ethernet adds collision detection. A transmitting station monitors the medium and can detect a collision while sending. We will use that wired shared-medium setting for the next steps. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet does not use this contention procedure, and Wi-Fi does not simply reuse wired Ethernet's collision-detection operation.
sections.takeaway: CSMA/CD belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not all modern Ethernet links.

sections.title: Detect, abort, and signal
sections.narration: When the collision reaches a transmitting station, it stops the unsuccessful frame transmission and sends a jam signal according to the Ethernet procedure. Both stations then enter a retry process. The jam is not the original data successfully reaching its destination. Its purpose belongs to collision handling, not to acknowledging receipt of the intended payload.
sections.takeaway: Collision detection limits time wasted on an already failed transmission.

sections.title: Why propagation affects frame length
sections.narration: Consider the farthest possible competing sender. A collision caused near the far end must propagate back while the original sender is still transmitting if that sender is to detect it. This motivates a relationship between minimum frame transmission time and the collision domain's extent. Exact Ethernet limits depend on the standard and physical configuration.
bullets: A far-end clash must return in time
sections.takeaway: Collision detection constrains the relation between frame time and network extent.

sections.title: Widen the random retry range
sections.narration: If both stations immediately restart after the jam, another clash is likely. Ethernet therefore uses randomized backoff. As repeated collisions occur, the choice range grows exponentially up to a cap. Each station independently chooses from the appropriate range. Waiting reduces synchronized retries, but it is a contention mechanism rather than a guaranteed reservation.
sections.takeaway: Binary exponential backoff expands the retry-choice range after collisions.

sections.title: Work two retry choices
sections.narration: In our example, the first collision gives each station a choice of zero or one backoff slot. After a second collision, choices range from zero through three. Let A choose one and B choose three. Their different delays help separate the next attempts. These backoff slots are Ethernet timing units, not ALOHA packet slots.
sections.takeaway: After two collisions, this example draws independently from four slot choices.

sections.title: Backoff does not reserve the cable
sections.narration: Even after choosing a waiting interval, a station has not booked a private future turn. Other stations may transmit, so the access procedure still has to account for the medium's state before the retry. Our chosen numbers illustrate separation, not guaranteed success. Repeated failures can ultimately cause the frame transmission attempt to be abandoned.
sections.takeaway: Finishing a backoff does not guarantee exclusive access.

sections.title: Modern switched full duplex
sections.narration: Replace the shared cable with separate full-duplex links to a switch. A host can transmit and receive at once on its link, without competing for the old shared half-duplex wire. CSMA/CD is not used on that full-duplex link. Queues, congestion, and dropped frames can still occur; removing collisions does not remove every network bottleneck.
sections.takeaway: Full-duplex switched Ethernet removes the shared-wire collision scenario.

sections.title: Wi-Fi needs different feedback
sections.narration: Wireless stations cannot assume they can reliably detect another transmission's collision while transmitting their own strong signal. Stations can also hear different neighbors. Wi-Fi therefore uses collision-avoidance mechanisms and acknowledgments, with additional details beyond this episode. Carrier sensing remains useful, but wired CSMA/CD is not an accurate description of Wi-Fi medium access.
bullets: Avoidance and ACKs help manage access
sections.takeaway: Wi-Fi uses collision-avoidance mechanisms rather than Ethernet-style CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Compare the added knowledge
sections.narration: Line up the three strategies. ALOHA starts without carrier sensing. CSMA checks local channel activity before attempting transmission. CSMA/CD also detects collisions during transmission in its appropriate wired setting. Each uses more information, but none makes signal propagation instantaneous. Keep the assumptions beside the diagram whenever you compare their behavior or efficiency.
sections.takeaway: Each improvement adds information while retaining physical limitations.

sections.title: Explain the next collision
sections.narration: Replay the opening clash. Now you can propose aligned slots, carrier sensing, or a wired detection-and-backoff procedure, and explain each approach's limits. Before answering an exam question, identify whether the system is shared half-duplex Ethernet, switched full duplex, or wireless. That context determines which collision story is physically and technically appropriate.
sections.takeaway: Medium-access behavior depends on both protocol rules and physical context.
